story: Lake Towada fills a double caldera that began to form with volcanic activity about 200,000 years ago. It is the third-deepest lake in Japan, and its shores and outer rim are still covered in natural forest. The lake has a single outlet, the Oirase River, which has cut a U-shaped valley fourteen kilometres long, its stream broken by rapids and waterfalls under natural forest. The lake and the gorge together are a Special Place of Scenic Beauty and a Natural Monument. North of them rise the Hakkoda Mountains, a volcanic group of eighteen peaks topped by Ōdake at 1,584 metres.

The Hachimantai half of the park, to the south, is one of Japan's great volcanic regions. Long volcanic activity and deep winter snow have left a high plateau of bogs and crater ponds such as Hachiman-numa, ringed by peaks: Hachimantai itself, Akita-Komagatake, and Iwate-san, the park's highest, whose lopsided profile is called Nanbu Kata-Fuji, the half-Fuji of Nanbu. On its north-east flank the Yakehashiri lava flow is still bare black rock. Heat rises everywhere: Goshogake bubbles with mud pots, and Tamagawa's spring, at pH 1.2, pours out 9,000 litres a minute.

Forests of beech cover the lower slopes and Maries' fir the higher ones, and in winter wind-driven snow and rime freeze the firs into the juhyō, the 'snow monsters' of Hakkoda and Hachimantai. Asiatic black bears (tsukinowaguma) feed on beech mast, and Japanese serow, a Special Natural Monument, live in the forests. Komakusa, a pink alpine poppy, grows in sheets on the volcanic gravel of Akita-Komagatake and the Yakehashiri route on Iwate-san.

People have long come to these mountains to bathe and to pray. Towada Shrine on the lake's south shore dates its worship to the Heian period; Tamagawa's spring was found by matagi hunters in the late 1600s; Sukayu, on the western flank of Hakkoda, has taken in bathers for about three hundred years. Hakkoda is also remembered for disaster: in January 1902, 199 of 210 soldiers on a winter training march died in a blizzard there. Towada National Park was designated in February 1936; the Hachimantai area was added in 1956, when the park took its present name.
howItWorks: The park is split into two areas of similar size across Aomori, Akita and Iwate prefectures: Towada-Hakkoda, 45,060 hectares, and Hachimantai, 40,474. Nearly all of it is national land — 80,133 of 85,534 hectares — with 1,348 hectares of public and 4,053 of private land. Among its sights are the lakeside village of Yasumiya and the mountain hot springs — Sukayu, Tsuta, the seven inns of Nyuto Onsen-kyō, and old tōji spas where guests still stay for days and cook for themselves.

About 13,288 hectares are special protection zone, where picking any plant, collecting fallen leaves or branches, catching animals or lighting a fire needs a permit from the Minister of the Environment. Another 68,165 hectares are special zone, where building, felling, quarrying and picking listed alpine plants need a permit, and only 4,081 hectares are ordinary zone. Vehicle-restriction areas on Hakkoda, Iwate-san and Akita-Komagatake keep snowmobiles and off-road vehicles off the mountains.

Traffic is managed at the busiest places. Aomori Prefecture is gradually taking cars off the road beside the Oirase stream: private cars were barred for a week in September 2026, all traffic for the first time on 13 September, with shuttle buses instead, and a bypass is being built so that the stream-side road can eventually close. On autumn mornings the viewing deck at Tsuta-numa can be entered only with an advance booking and a conservation fee. On Akita-Komagatake the road to the eighth-station car park is open only to buses, taxis and two-wheelers on weekends and holidays from June to October, and every day from late June to mid-August. Five of the park's volcanoes — Hakkoda, Towada, Akita-Yakeyama, Iwate-san and Akita-Komagatake — are watched around the clock by the Japan Meteorological Agency.

sightNotes.poi-jp-towada-hachimantai-lake-towada: A deep caldera lake with sightseeing boats from Yasumiya, canoe tours, Towada Shrine and the Maidens statue on the south shore.
sightNotes.poi-jp-towada-hachimantai-oirase-gorge: Fourteen kilometres of stream, waterfalls and mossy boulders below the lake, with a riverside path the whole way from Nenokuchi to Yakeyama.
sightNotes.poi-jp-towada-hachimantai-hakkoda-odake: The highest of the Hakkoda volcanoes, 1,584 metres, reached on foot from Sukayu or the top of the Hakkoda Ropeway. Snow monsters in winter.
sightNotes.poi-jp-towada-hachimantai-tsuta-numa: A pond in the beech forest near Tsuta Onsen, famous for reflecting red autumn leaves at dawn. Early-morning entry in peak season is booked.
sightNotes.poi-jp-towada-hachimantai-hachimantai-an: A flat volcanic summit with raised bogs and a crater pond, reached by a short path from the car park on the Aspite Line.
sightNotes.poi-jp-towada-hachimantai-goshogake-onse: A hot-spring inn with mud baths, next to a nature trail through steaming ground, mud pots and Japan's largest mud volcano.
sightNotes.poi-jp-towada-hachimantai-iwate-san: The park's highest peak, a stratovolcano with a crater-rim path lined with Kannon statues and the bare Yakehashiri lava flow on its flank.
sightNotes.poi-jp-towada-hachimantai-akita-komagata: A group of volcanic peaks topped by Onamedake, 1,637 metres, with meadows of komakusa and other alpine flowers.

planYourVisit.reservations: Early-morning entry to the Tsuta-numa viewing deck in the autumn colour season must be booked and paid for in advance. Private cars are barred from the Oirase road on set days in September and from the Akita-Komagatake road on summer weekends, holidays and high-summer weekdays. Dates change each year: check before you go with Towada city, Aomori Prefecture and Senboku city.
permits: No permit is needed for the park's trails; crater areas close when a volcano's alert level rises

chronology.text: Volcanic activity begins that will form the double caldera of Lake Towada.
In January, 199 of 210 soldiers on a winter march in the Hakkoda Mountains die in a blizzard.
Towada National Park is designated on 1 February.
The Hachimantai area is added and the park is renamed Towada-Hachimantai.
Vehicle-restriction areas are designated on Hakkoda, Iwate-san and Akita-Komagatake.
Heavy rain in August sends debris onto the Oirase stream path, which reopens in full in September.
On 13 September the road beside the Oirase stream is closed to all traffic for the first time, a step towards taking it off the gorge for good.

safety: Volcanic gas can collect in hollows around Hakkoda, Hachimantai and the hot-spring areas. Stay on marked paths and obey closure signs. Hakkoda, Towada, Akita-Yakeyama, Iwate-san and Akita-Komagatake are monitored by the Japan Meteorological Agency; check the alert level before climbing.
Asiatic black bears (tsukinowaguma) are common in the beech forests. Make noise, carry bear spray, and check recent sightings at the visitor centres.
Winter in the mountains is severe and the back-country is easy to get lost in; go with a guide. The 1902 Hakkoda march is the classic warning.
The Oirase path and mountain roads can close after heavy rain.
regulations: Do not pick alpine plants such as komakusa; listed species are protected throughout the special zones.
Picking any plant, collecting fallen branches, catching animals or lighting a fire in the special protection zone needs a permit.
Follow the seasonal private-car restrictions on the Oirase road and the Akita-Komagatake road.
Snowmobiles and off-road vehicles are barred from the vehicle-restriction areas on Hakkoda, Iwate-san and Akita-Komagatake.

weather: Snow is the defining fact of the place. Sukayu, at about 900 metres, can lie under five metres of it, and from January to February the Hakkoda and Hachimantai firs turn into snow monsters and the powder draws back-country skiers. Spring comes late: the Aspite Line opens in April between walls of snow, and new leaves then fill the Oirase Gorge. Summer is cool in the mountains, with alpine flowers on Akita-Komagatake. Autumn is the busiest season, when the beech forests around Lake Towada, Oirase and Tsuta-numa turn colour.
directions: For Lake Towada and Hakkoda, take the Tohoku Shinkansen to Shin-Aomori (about 3 hours 10 minutes from Tokyo), then the seasonal JR bus via the Hakkoda Ropeway (about 1 hour 15 minutes) and the Oirase Gorge to the lake (about 2 hours 50 minutes). For Hachimantai, take the Tohoku Shinkansen to Morioka for seasonal buses up to the plateau, or the Akita Shinkansen to Tazawako for buses to Nyuto Onsen and Akita-Komagatake. Aomori, Hanamaki and Akita airports serve the region. Many park roads close in winter; a car makes the most sense outside it.
